utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic, Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, last night we proofed this witness, and we can begin our examination-in-chief today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed. Examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, would you introduce yourself to us.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Mihic. I come from the village of Drinjaca in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Branko, could you please tell us your first and last name and spell it for the record.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. M-i-h-i-c diacritic. B-r-a-n-k-o.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us when and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: On the 29th of May, 1968, in Gornji Vuksic, the municipality of Brcko, Bosnia and Herzegovina, then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us briefly what the course of your career was.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I was born in Gornji Vuksic. My father was a teacher there. I lived there for a year and then we moved to Drinjaca where I still live today. On completion of elementary school, I enrolled in the military secondary school in Belgrade. I went to that school for two years and then I was expelled. After that I continued my schooling in Zvornik. I completed the secondary commercial school. After that I worked in Zagreb for a time. Then I came home, and in 1991 I got married. Now I'm a professional beekeeper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you said that you had been expelled from the military secondary school. Was the reason something you did or was there any other reason why you left that school?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I liked this school. That's why I enrolled in it. However, the circumstances were such that the -- the official reason given for my expulsion was one thing, and I think the real reason was something else. In that school we wore civilian clothes, although it was a military secondary school, and we could do whatever we wanted with our civilian clothes, and I sold mine at the market. This was quite usual. The reason I was expelled was that in 1985 at Drinjaca there was an organisation, a kind of Chetnik organisation. It later transpired that this was actually not the troika Chetnik organisation. My father was called as a witness, and there was pressure on him to give false testimony, and he refused, and I think that's why I was expelled from school. And there were a lot of sanctions against me in that system. I wanted to go and enroll in the medical secondary school, but I wasn't allowed to. I wasn't accepted. So I had to go to the commercial school, which I didn't like at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can only slow down a little bit for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before 1991, were you duty-bound to serve in the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I did not do my military service. In the laws of the former Yugoslavia, people who enrolled in military schools or academies and stayed there for more than two years didn't have to do their military service. I found this information in the newspaper, and I showed it to the people in the military department, and then they took this into account and didn't send me to do military service. However, a comrade of mine who was also expelled from the school like me did have to do his military service. So I was lucky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one point that since 1991, you have been employed in a private business and that you are a professional beekeeper. Can you explain this, Mr. Mihic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Beekeeping as a profession is not covered by taxes and is not something that you register. So I do not have a registered business. I am a farmer, I can say that, and I have 200 beehives and that's how I earn my living. That's how I support my family. Only that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When the war broke out in Zvornik, did you become active in the military?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Before the wartime conflicts broke out in Zvornik, I went to the Mali Zvornik barracks, to Dragan Obrenovic's unit, only for the sake of the salary. The salaries were good. There was nothing to do there. The work wasn't hard. I was married. I had a child. I was unemployed. I did keep bees at the time, but only as a hobby. So the only reason I joined that unit was for the salary. When the Yugoslav army withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina, that unit left Mali Zvornik and I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that when you got to know Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us. That year, how long did you stay in Mali Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. Perhaps two months at the most. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. On your return to Zvornik, what did you do next with regard to joining the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Drinjaca, I joined the ordinary village patrol. It wasn't really a unit. When the battalion was established, I joined the signals department in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you trained for communications?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during those wartime years did you manage to learn the work of a signalsman?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to tell us how you advanced in this Signals Unit and what duties you performed in the Signals Unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, when the signals squad was set up, I worked at the switchboard, the radio switchboard. My komandir was the late Borko. He was a sergeant. Borko Vukajlovic, who, when he went to Bratunac to attend a meeting about communications, was killed in Kravica in 1991. After he was killed, I took over the duty of komandir. We had communications with all the units, all the companies, mostly telephone communications, radio communications, but not so much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment. Who was the commander of the battalion to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Dragon Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After this how did you advance in this job?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: When the wartime operations in Drinjaca were over, my battalion went on toward Bratunac above Konjevic Polje. I was transferred to Malisic from there. This is a place which is about 40 kilometres away from Drinjaca, below Zvornik. And I was also the komandir, the commander of the signals unit in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From when to when were you the komandir of the signals department in Malisic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think it was in 1993. I don't think it went on into 1994, but I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the battalion commander at that time if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think it was Nenad Simic. After he left it was Radenko Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After performing this duty in 1993, where were you transferred after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I was far away from my home and my native village, and I kept insisting that I be transferred back. Dragan Obrenovic then decided to help me, and I was transferred to the Zvornik Brigade, to Standard. And there are I became the komandir of a unit. It was the so-called Mlada Vojska, Young Troops, and there were 14 of us. And all we did actually was clean the corridors and the toilets. That's all we did. We didn't do anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you said that you got this better position thanks to Dragan Obrenovic, where there was practically no work to do.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I explained to him it was difficult for me to travel 40 or 50 kilometres through snow and rain without any vehicle, and he decided to grant my request. The new chief of communications --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: -- who arrived in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the interpreters didn't catch the name of the new chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. From the transcript I did not see the names. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your intervention, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, could you please tell us who, then, became the chief of communications?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Gaborovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was Dragan Obrenovic's duty at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: He was then the chief of staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The commander was Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Obrenovic as the chief of staff have the right to transfer you from one post to another?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think he did, but it wasn't a personal order from him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you trying to say by this, "it wasn't a personal order from him"? It was his authority, but someone else issued the order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this. I don't want to put a leading question. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I asked him about this but it wasn't him who wrote out the order. Probably there were no written traces at all. He said, "Mihic, from tomorrow you're going to Standard, and you'll be working there." That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Obrenovic have that kind of authority at the time? Could he just say to the chief of communications, "Well, transfer this man"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And according to the system, who was supposed to issue the order about your transfer from one duty to another?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it was my chief of communications, because if I had come from Drinjaca it was logical for them to send me back, but he was the one who assigned people to various posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he do that pursuant to an order from Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after that you moved to where?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: When I got there, I stayed there for about two months or maybe a month. But I didn't do anything there, absolutely nothing. And then I asked -- I said, "Well, I'm not just a broom you can send to sweep wherever you want." And then I was transferred to the radio relay centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since when did you work at the radio relay centre as a signalsman? From what date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the date, but it was in 1994, 1995. That's when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the komandir of that signals department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Radio communication, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as the commander of the squad, of this communications squad, did you do that job in July 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at that post doing that work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I might have stayed -- well, I can't say exactly, but it might have been August of that year, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps this is a good opportunity to ask you the following question: The signals squad, how many people were there to that unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, the number of people changed, but there were always between four and eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you in July 1995, physically?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The command post of the brigade was in the Standard factory. That was common knowledge. So we were one kilometre up the hill from that command post, one kilometre away in a metal container.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what communication devices and signals devices did you have in that metal container up on the hill?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: They were the devices that belonged to my squad, the RUP 12, and a radio station. I think it was all the RRU 100, but we referred to it as the 100. But it belonged to the other squad that was next to ours, and they had the RRU 800 device. And of course a telephone line with the brigade command, an inductor telephone. A wire connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you organise the work at this radio relay centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, it changed, catering to the needs whether there was two, two or three, three, or if we needed 100 per cent men on the job we'd all be there. If there was any combat operations, all of us were there 100 per cent. If not, we would take shifts and relieve each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Establishment-wise, who did you belong to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: We belonged to the signals company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the signals company in July?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The commander was Radic Dragisa or Dragisa Radic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you said that you had a telephone line or a wire communication, as you put it, I think, with the brigade command. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, and explain what kind of telephone line that was for us laymen who are not professional soldiers and signalsmen. What does an inductor telephone that you mentioned actually mean? What was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The brigade command was put up at the Standard on the first floor, I think. Upstairs on the second floor there was the telephone switchboard, the exchange, and the exchange operator were both men and women. And then from that switchboard there was a wire stretched to me and the wire was about 1.000 metres, and it was attached to the telephone. So from my radio relay centre, using an inductor I could call up the switchboard and exchange and they could then connect me to anywhere, any battalion, any town, any country. They could put me through anywhere I wanted to speak to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you didn't have a direct telephone line with the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a wire connection, telephone inductor connection, with the battalions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Only through the switchboard. Exclusively through the switchboard. The radio centre, the switchboard, and then out to anyplace I wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, did you have any telephone wire inductor connection with the superior commands, the Drina Corps and the Main Staff directly? Did you have a direct line to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Through the switchboard, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you had this inductor telephone line directly only to the switchboard which was located at the command of the Zvornik Brigade? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. So when I used the inductor telephone, it would be the switchboard that answers me. Nobody else could answer me, just the switchboard. It went through straight to the exchange, to the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to radio communications now. You said that you had the RUP 12 device; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for us laymen who don't know what this is about, what kind of device it is, could you explain what the RUP 12 is, what its range is.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It was a piece of equipment -- how could I explain this to you? Ten or 12 kilogrammes with two types of antennae, a long one and a short one with different ranges. And it depended an optic sight [as interpreted]. The larger the optic site, the further the frequency, which does not mean that you couldn't get a connection within a space of three kilometres. There were depression and elevations and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you yourself, on the -- with this radio device, did you have a connection to the battalion?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The location I was at the with the radio devices wasn't selected at random. It was the sole case where I could have a connection with all the battalions. If I were to move ten metres to the left or ten metres to the right I wouldn't have this connection. So this was this spot, this particular location that allowed me to have radio communication with all the battalions, and I could hear and communicate with them at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we had a commander, for example, or an operative unit working in the field at any given time carrying another RUP 12 device with them, if they had a RUP 12, then with these mobile radio devices could you achieve a communication as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not in all cases. Not in all circumstances. If somebody was standing in a depression with a RUP, then I couldn't reach him, which doesn't mean that he couldn't reach me by another battalion, going via another battalion and reaching me in that way, a roundabout way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have radio communication with the superior units, that is to say with the command of the Drina Corps, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Radio communications with the command of the Drina Corps never functioned. It was never operational, never. The RRU 100 device was used. You could hear very badly through it, and it never worked, hardly ever worked. So not really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you about those radio devices and means of communications in the Zvornik Brigade. You said, I believe, that at the command of the brigade, on the upper storey was where the switchboard was located; is that the?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was this? What kind of communication did they have, the people operating the switchboard?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The switchboard was linked to all the battalions by a wire connection. So at all times you could use the inductor telephone from the battalions and reach the switchboard, anybody at all. There was a relay device too. I don't know much about that and I don't know its name either, whether it was called the VZ something and a number after it. But that was a relay device, and that was used, but I really don't know how because I'm not well-versed in that particular device.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the process and procedure the same when you went externally or somebody rang up the Zvornik Brigade from outside? Would it have to go through that switchboard and then be connected to the person that they wanted to speak to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think there were two numbers. One number was the one we referred to as the civilian number at the switchboard which you would phone up, and then you would be connected anywhere, the command of the brigade, the command of the battalion. And then there was a direct telephone line at the command itself. I can't remember the telephone number. I did know it by heart, but I just can't remember it now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question to you is this: Could you help us out, please. Somebody is calling from the Drina Corps, for example, and he wants to speak to the duty operations man in the brigade. How can he reach the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: If he's calling from the Drina Corps, he could call up the switchboard and say, "I want to speak to the duty officer," and then he switches two switches and connects him to the duty operations officer. Or he can phone him on that fixed telephone number directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This fixed telephone number, could it be intercepted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think so. I think this could be tapped into, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the other number, the one going through the switchboard? Could that be tapped into?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the same. It would be the same case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your radio communications through the RUP 12, could that be intercepted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. You could intercept anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you as the komandir of that radio centre, radio signals or communications centre, did you know whether the conversations you had through RUP 12 could be intercepted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that because I intercepted conversations from the opposite side. I did the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the procedure when regular and interim combat reports were sent out through the superior units? Which devices would be used? How could you do that? How would the combat reports, regular or interim, be sent out and distributed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: In the communications centre there were four squads and you had the encoding department, you had the telephonists, you had the radio operators and the radio relay operators. We ourselves did not send out reports of that kind. Those were sent out by the encoders, encrypters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where the encrypters or encoders were located, that is to state people who would send out regular combat reports, for example?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: They were located, I think, on the same floor where the switchboard was in another separate office. In the brigade command in the Standard buildings, on the Standard premises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were they in a separate room? Why weren't they by the switchboard?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It was a special department for encryption, encoding. Nobody was allowed to enter except them and the commander. It was highly secretive, highly confidential. Let me just say that from the colleagues that worked there -- it had nothing to do with my department, but I asked them and tried what -- to see what they were doing, but I wasn't allowed to go in and have a look. They didn't give me permission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we understand each other, who was the sole person able to enter the encryption department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: As far as I gathered from them, the sole person was the commander. Only the commander could enter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like to -- you to explain using a practical example of how this functioned, and I'd like to ask the usher's help for an exhibit that we've already used here. It was Prosecution Exhibit P519, and it was a regular combat report of the Zvornik Brigade dated the 14th of July, 1995. Mr. Mihic, you have before you a document. It is titled Regular Combat Report from the Zvornik Brigade on the 14th of July, 1995, sent out to the command of the Drina Corps. It was sent by the commander Major Dragan Obrenovic, and it was sent on the 14th of July, 1995, at 1840 hours. Can you see that? You have it in front of you. At the stamp at the bottom, if you take a look. And you have the signature, V. Stojkic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, who V. Stojkic was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Vinko Stojkic. He was an operator in that encryption department. I think he was also the komandir of that squad or department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he one of the people who was permitted to be in the encryption office?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, once a report of this kind is written out, how is it sent on to the encryption department?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the witness said before he wasn't involved in this process of sending these reports, and also the information he gave us about the entry into this encryption room was sort of secondhand. So I would like to object to anything -- going into details about the process he isn't aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, would you please ask this once again whether he was involved in the sending of the reports to lay some foundation for this question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, at one point you said that you were interested, from your signals, fellow signalsmen, to learn of the way in which the encryption, encrypters worked?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did they tell you the kinds of situations that they would be able to send out a document of this kind? Does it have to be authorised and signed by the commander or what?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell me that, but based on my experience, I think it would have to have been signed and authorised by the commander. So this isn't my sphere. But as far as I know, the report and document would have to be signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And following on from that context, I want to ask you the following: Were you ever in a position that through your radio centre this kind of confidential, strictly confidential reports were ever sent out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. We never sent reports of this kind out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, my question to you -- my next question is why.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a reliable communication and line. And there was no need. They had a wire connection if they were in the field. If you were two kilometres away you could use the telephone and ring up. So there was no reason and no need to use that, and everything was intercepted and tapped into. So that wasn't standard practice at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: An experienced officer, an experienced commander, would he do something like this knowing that the radio communication is intercepted? Would they sent such document through you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is pure speculation to ask him what an experienced commander would do or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It is a speculative question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll go back to more concrete things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tour of duty, was any regular or interim report sent via your radio centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the second part of the questions that are relative to communication. You were in the radio communication centre, and you wanted to say something or communicate something to the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you do it using the RUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that the duty operations officer did not have another RUP 12 on him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it means. He didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you have to communicate to him. You have to pass on certain information that you had received from the battalion. How did you do that? How did you communicate to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: If I received information, I will speak to the duty operations man at the switchboard who will pass it on. Or I would call the switchboard and I would ask to speak to the duty operations officer. That was the alternative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to ask you. One of the battalions - and we have a logbook of the duty operations officers recording the requirements for equipment, ammunition and so on and so forth - one of the battalion addressed you and asked you to inform the logistics that they needed ammunition, batteries, Browning ammunition and similar things. How would you pass on this information to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: If this was asked from me, I would call the switchboard and I will pass the information on, and they in their turn will pass the information on to the duty operations officers. I could try and contact the duty operations officer myself, but he was not always in his office. So I would rather call the switchboard and ask them to pass on the information on to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be more practical because somebody was always at the switchboard at all times?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There was always somebody at the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you passed on the information to the person working at the switchboard, how would that person communicate that to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It would be done on foot. It would be written on a piece of paper and that person would literally take it downstairs to the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you yourself did not have to communicate that information directly to the duty informations -- duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were working in -- at the radio communications centre, what was the common practice? Was it the common practice for you to communicate to the duty operations officer directly or did you leave the information with the person at the switchboard who would then bring it to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It was easier for me to leave the information with the switchboard operator who would then bring it to the duty operations officer. It was much easier, more practical for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same question, but let's go to the superior command. We're now talking -- we were now talking about the battalion, but let's go to the superior command. In the duty operations officer logbook it says "Beara to report to 155." Somebody's asking from the duty operations officer for this information to be passed on to Beara. What would the procedure be in this case? Did you have to talk to the duty operations officer directly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. We could simply call the switchboard and ask them to pass the information on, and they would do it at the first opportunity. So we didn't have to speak to the duty operations officer himself. It could be done through the switchboard operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Does it mean that bearing in mind the system of communications, the duty operations officer did not necessarily have to receive directly any such information, any such request?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: That's correct. It wasn't the duty operations officer who received that. It would be the switchboard operator who would receive that, put it on a piece of paper and take it physically to the duty operations officer who was supposed to receive it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And wouldn't that be the job of the communications or signalsmen, the branch that you belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. That wouldn't be my job. There would be other people, people who are switchboard operators who would do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within this system of communication via the switchboard, could the duty operations officer be in the position to receive information more often through the switchboard or directly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: More often he would receive it from the switchboard because everything went via the switchboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me ask you about your position, the position that you had up there as the radio communications squad. Why did you exist if there were radio and telephone lines?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: We were on a stand-by if telephone lines did not work. So we worked very rarely. Within the period of 12 hours, we would maybe check our connection once and that was -- that was it. Over the next five days, maybe we did not even hear each other once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your function? Was your function to establish communication was those units or those officers who at that given moment did not have a telephone line?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. If the telephone communication was broken, then it would be us that established communication links. And if the units were on a move, in combat, then we would be mediators. We would mediate in their communication because they could communicate directly, and they did it on a daily basis. When that was not possible, we would mediate in their communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th and 14th there was fighting in the area of the Zvornik Brigade. Certain units were transferred to Snagovo. We have heard a lot of testimonies about that. Did you have communication with those units in Snagovo? Did you establish a radio connection with them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm just objecting to using specific examples which are not correct. For instance, there was no fighting on the 13th. So that's a generalisation. I don't know whether it's needed, it's important for the purposes of this question, but if he does it, it needs to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I did not understand this remark. The first ambush and the first conflict with the column and the military police of the Zvornik Brigade happened on the 13th, and on the 14th in the evening there was the most fierce fighting with the ambush of Snagovo. We have heard testimonies to that effect. If that is not correct, as my learned friend says, then I will also accept that there was no fighting on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. Here the suggestion is not that there was fighting on the 13th or the 14th. Here we just want to establish whether this person has some connection with the unit there. These are the most important things, no matter whether there is fighting or not. So let's concentrate on that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was the goal of my question. However, an objection was raised to the effect that there was into fighting on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is as follows: On the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, the 16th of July, during those developments and events did you have -- your squad that is, the radio communications squad -- did you have -- did you establish a link with those units which were on the move?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this communication function or would it be interrupted from time to time because those units were on the move?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It worked at times, and at times it didn't work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now I wanted to ask you something very specific. Can you remember on the 14th, in the night between the 14th and 15th and on the 15th, were you in the communications centre and up to when?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I believe I wasn't. It was a long time ago. On the 15th, however, I was absent because my wife was due to give birth. The road to Drinjaca was closed because of these combat activities, so I had to go via Serbia. I had to cross the Drina. I had to go and fetch my wife, and I had to bring my wife and two young children to Zvornik, to my sister's place. And then I returned to the communications centre, but I don't know when that was. It was a long time ago. But I was there. There were combat operations. I was on the line. I may have been absent for three or four hours, but I had to. The road was blocked. There were two young children at home. My wife was pregnant and about to give birth, so my family needed me, and that's why I left the position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when it was that you left on the 15th of July for these objective reasons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was sometime in the morning. The 15th of July was the date when she was due, and I just left on the 15th of July to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of these combat activities, you can conclude that you were there in your position on the 14th and 15th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were you organised at the time, in view of the intensive fighting in the area of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I believe that we were all there, on the line. A hundred per cent of the troops were there. Mind you, only one person could actually work. The rest of us were probably sitting watching TV while that one person was working.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that you were aware that what you were doing could be intercepted and was indeed intercepted by the enemy, can you tell us how would it happen within the system if you were to pass on a piece of intelligence to a battalion or to the units on the move? Did you have certain codes, code names? Did you have the means to carry out secret conversations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we received our communications plans, we also received codes that every battalion had. For example, one letter would be replaced by three or four figures or several letters. So when a piece of information was to be communicated, we would receive a lot of numbers. For example, 562 was letter B. For example, if I were to sent confidential information, I would just send the other person a cluster of numbers. The person who received it, he would just follow those numbers and that's how he could decipher the text. It was very rarely that this was used, because we could normally avail ourselves of the wire lines, of the telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you as the commander of that communications squad have an opportunity or were you given a task to give one of your soldiers to Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. My unit was the one that gave soldiers to Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain how this functioned? How did your soldiers serve under him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: For example, a RUP 12 would be taken from the depot. The soldier would put it on his back, literally. And if Dragan Obrenovic was sent to the field, then that soldier would literally follow him. And that soldier had to be very fit, because not everybody could follow Obrenovic when he was moving around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember on the 14th of July who was escorting him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was Milos Pantic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 14th and the 15th of July, was he with him all the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to RUP 12, did Dragan Obrenovic also use or could he use the UK device [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: He usually carried a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Motorola, do you mean that a Motorola is a UKT device?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he use his Motorola in order to establish a direct link with the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To be more specific, let me ask you: Could he use his Motorola to dispatch information to the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, he could not. He couldn't do it directly. He could via somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this mean that the duty operations officer did not have a Motorola available?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the usher to assist us to show the witness exhibit for identification, Your Honour. It's P520, and this is a document we have already had an occasion to see. It's an interim combat report of the 14th of July, 1995, which was used by Mr. Butler and also by us when examining Witness Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, would you please look at the text of this interim combat report and tell us to whom it's addressed. What does it say?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: "To the command of the Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And who signed this document? Who is sending it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Major Dragan Obrenovic, chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The questions answers are following so quickly, so I may not have a chance to object. But again, if he asked this witness to comment on some substantive text, I have a problem. If he asks him again whether somebody, you know, signed this document who was part of his squad, that's no problem. But to have him again speculate about what may be here, then I have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think the issue is here that whether you could establish a certain kind of relevancy between this document and this witness. That is to say whether this witness is in the position to make some comments of that document. And before that, we shall not go into the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There is no need for hasty objections. I do not intend to ask the witness to comment on this interim combat report. My questions will be in a completely different direction, and we will link this all up through the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's just familiarise ourselves with the document and then I'll put questions to you. The document says: "Tonight at around 2020 hours, a large group of Muslims passed through the broader Maricici area, proceeding towards the Zvornik-Caparde road." And I won't read any more although it's brief. I'll just read the last bit. The second paragraph says: "Try to find some means of bringing in more intervention forces early in the morning." And then it's signed by Dragan Obrenovic. Would you, sir -- Mr. Mihic, look at the seal --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Waespi, I don't think the question has been asked yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not signed by Mr. Obrenovic. That's what he keeps referring. So that's a misstatement of facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we say that in the document, at the place where it is stated who is sending the document, it's true there is no signature, but that was not the purpose of my question. We've already established all this through the testimony of Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, what I wanted to ask was the following: Would you please look at the seal with me, at the stamp, saying when the document was sent.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think it's 0110 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Again I really object to this witness who wasn't involved in sending these documents, who was at a hill outside Zvornik to comment on a document, on dates. The document speaks for itself. And we have here Mr. Bojanovic. These people were qualified to comment on it, not this witness, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this stage I actually have not heard the substantive questions put by Mr. Stojanovic. I believe that Mr. Stojanovic is now just laying some background. But let's come to see the question you're going to ask this witness. And you told us before that it will be a quite different direction. We'll see how different it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, until last night when I showed this document to you, had you ever seen it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. I see Vinko Stojkic signed it, so it couldn't have been sent through me. It must have been sent through the encryption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll show you a part of the statement made by Dragan Obrenovic, the statement of facts before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it might be more practical to put this on the ELMO - it's a public document - so that we can see the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In his statement, Dragan Obrenovic mentions this document and says: "That same evening, 14th between 2300 hours and 0000 hours, I wrote a request to the Drina Corps command for results on a piece of paper and I gave it to my signalsman. He in turn sent the message to the radioman. It was transmitted to the communication centre and then relayed to the duty officer, Dragan Jokic. This was after the battles and the capture of police captain Zoran Jankovic." My question, Mr. Mihic, is as follows: On the 14th of July while you were in the radio centre, at any point in time did you receive this kind of open telegram from Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: There needs to be a foundation whether this person was there on the 14th. I think he testified earlier he was away for three hours. So before he goes in to basically assuming, he should establish the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe the witness testified before that he was not stay there for the whole day. He was absent for some time. So the first question is that, you know, from what time, you know, this witness was absent during that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The witness did state, and you can see on the previous page, that he left on the 15th of July, before noon. And in answer to my next question, he said that in the night between the 14th and 15th, he was there at the radio centre and that they were all present there because of the intensive fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That was a general answer he testified in these present, but he specifically said he was off and on. So I don't think it's correct to assume now that on that night he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, since there's some, you know, different interpretations, would you please ask some questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, a few minutes ago we discussed this. Would you tell us when you went to pick up your wife in Drinjaca, who was about to give birth.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand me. This was a long time ago. I think I left on the 15th because she was due to give birth on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: At what time on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: If it was the 15th, it was in the morning. It was before noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I crossed the bridge over the Drina. I went into Serbia by boat. I crossed the Drina by boat. And then I took my wife and children to Serbia, to Mali Zvornik, to be with my sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 15th in the morning, how long were you away from the radio centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Three or four hours, because I was in a hurry. I had to be on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then return to the radio centre?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the day before, the 14th, and the night between the 14th and the 15th, did you spend that time together with the others in the squad?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the radio centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: Between 2300 hours and 0000 hours on the 14th, did you receive through the open RUP communication this interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't, but please don't misunderstand me. There were four of us there. Maybe somebody else did, but I did not. Although I'm not familiar with this text; we read whatever arrived, but I don't remember seeing this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you said that you never received such documents through the RUP open line.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. Especially not from the commander of the chief of staff. This was never sent through us. We were there to communicate with the battalions. It was the battalions who would send their reports through us, and these were usually very trivial. They would just say "Situation as usual." The battalions would sometimes send their reports to me if the lines were down, and this would usually read just "Situation normal."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive from the commander or the chief of staff the task of sending such an important document through the open communication?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. The commander never called on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I propose that we take a break now. I will put a few more questions about the witness's knowledge of Dragan Jokic and then that would conclude my examination-in-chief. I will need not more than ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the break, and we will resume at quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Mihic, I now have a few questions to ask you about Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since when have you known Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I've known Dragan Jokic since he was the chief of staff of the brigade, that is to say at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet him perhaps during the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see him talk to other soldiers, conversing to other officers, superior officers, subordinate officers, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what your impressions are of Dragan Jokic and what the troops and soldiers thought of him? What were their comments?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I'll be frank. I'll tell you what I really think. I think most of the people here whom I don't know here have not read a novel called "Nikoletina Bursac" who is also the main character. At first chance he is a rather rough-looking type, rough-looking character but with a very kind heart and soul. He loved everything, loved nature and loved everything that was civilised, just as the character in the book "Nikoletina Bursac." As you know, my profession is a beekeeper, and Dragan Jokic bought some bees from me, and he gave me his official pistol for what were practically two empty beehives. It was just the same as if he'd given it to me in exchange for two boxes of cigarettes, for example. Dragan Jokic knew I was a hunter, and he had a rifle. I don't know what kind it was, but he wanted to give it to me as a gift. That was before any of these events took place. So quite simply I can say that he was a good man. He wasn't a careerist, a career oriented. But the officers persecuted him, mistreated him, didn't treat him properly, and I found that difficult to take. But what can you do? That's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever in a situation in which you attended these conversations and communications between Dragan Jokic and his superior officers when they behaved towards him that way, with a lack of respect, or undermined him and the man he was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and I found it shameful to be in their company when they took it out on them, the superior officers took it out on him in front of other soldiers, in front of the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be more specific and tell us how they berated him and undermined him, the superior officers?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I was present on one occasion when the commanding officer asked him to dig a communicating trench. He said I don't want anybody else, any other soldier to dig the trench, I want you to do it. So he took up a shovel and started digging this communicating trench. He didn't have to do for long, but it was just to prove a point and the way they treated him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion while you were working as a signalsman near the command of the Zvornik Brigade to hear from the soldiers or the citizens members of the Zvornik Brigade anything about Dragan having taken part in any crimes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. I'd never heard anything like that about Dragan's participation in any crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you hear about the crimes generally that were committed in the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I was a signalsman up at the signals department. And believe me when I say I didn't hear anything about those crimes, not a single letter. I heard about it when everything became public. But otherwise, there was never any mention of anything of that kind and I knew absolutely nothing about anything like that at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you know about his family situation, Dragan Jokic's family situation, his family circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I knew his financial situation and his family situation, although we weren't close. We weren't friends. We didn't actually -- but we did socialise a bit. I think he's divorced. He had to look after a son, I think. I think it was his second or third marriage. I know he has a very fine young son, a very cultivated, nice young man. I know he lived in somebody else's apart. He was a tenant. That's all I can say. That's all I know about him. But I do know that the other officers gained a great deal more than he did. He wasn't interested in anything material, whereas the other officers accrued more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mihic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours; good morning, sir. I have no questions for the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I have just a few questions, and I have been using one exhibit, Exhibit P121. I'm sorry I didn't announce it previously. That's the own exhibit I will be using, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes please. Cross-examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mihic. I have just a few issues I'd like to clarify with you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me first go back to your whereabouts. This morning Mr. Stojanovic had asked you, and I quote him: "And now I wanted to ask you something very specific. Can you remember on the 14th, in the night between the 14th and the 15th and on the 15th, were you in the communications centre and up to when? " And your answer was: "I believe I wasn't. It was a long time ago." And then you go on to talk about the 15th. Now, you don't really know where you were in those days because it's such a long time ago. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think this question has been asked and answered, but we would like to hear the witness once again. Yes. I understand that. Let the witness answer that question. Yes. Is there anything that you still want to raise? If you have, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one sentence. I think, Your Honour, that not at one point did the witness say he was not there, but let the witness answer the question again. But then it would be proper to have the whole answer given by the witness quoted. It would be proper vis-a-vis the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The problem, Mr. President, is the question Mr. Stojanovic had asked, because it included 14th, 15th night, and I just would like to clarify what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You may proceed. Witness, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Fine. Whether I was there on the 14th, is that it? Well, I can't say 100 per cent. I think I was there. Now, if somebody were to ask you where were you two and a half years ago, it would be difficult for you to answer. So all I can say is I think I was there, but as the war was going on, I was at the front line 100 per cent. If I had gone to fetch my wife on the 15th, I actually deserted to go and fetch my wife and take her to be -- to give birth. So on the 14th I can say that 90 per cent, I'm sure 90 per cent that I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you just told us, in your words, that you deserted to get your wife. Did you ask authority then from somebody or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't ask anybody's permission, because it was a -- I had two sons, born in 1993 and 1994. My wife was nine months pregnant. She was full term. I had to go and fetch her from Zvornik in the morning. The road was impassable. So it was a life-or-death situation. I had to go to the Drina, across the Drina, go to Zvornik, bring my wife back. But my job didn't suffer. There were four or five signalsmen and just one device. So that wasn't a problem at all. I was the komandir and I assessed that I could go and get my wife without any problems. So my job didn't suffer at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the night 14th, 15th before you went to see your wife? Were you sleeping at all that night?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Probably I was. I don't know. I can't say. There were enough of us there. Somebody was always awake. There was always somebody manning the device, so it couldn't be left without anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in those time, 14th, 15th, 16th, there was a time, was it not, that the city of Zvornik, the town, was threatened by the Muslim forces? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the commander, the acting commander, the chief of staff Obrenovic, he was in the field and was trying to cope with that situation. Is that also a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: All right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you listen to open communication between the brigade duty officer and the corps asking desperately for measures how to cope with the situation? Do you remember those type of conversations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. No, I wasn't able to listen in to that. I couldn't listen in to that communication. I was on the other side. That was a different line altogether. I was from the brigade to the battalion, that connection, not brigade corps line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody else from your squad was able to -- to listen in to those kind of communications?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, not from my mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your squad wasn't -- wasn't doing that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, perhaps you can help us a little bit about the call-signs. Do you remember who Omega was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about Lovac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I think that was me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Lovac 1?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Chief of staff. When he goes into the field, he uses our call-sign and adds a 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember the call-sign or the real name of the person Celik, C-e-l-i-k? Do you remember who that was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have any exchanges with Obrenovic, being Lovac 1? You Lovac, Obrenovic Lovac 1. Did you have any exchanges on those critical days, let's say the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: There probably was something, but I can't be sure what. I can't say exactly. Probably there was some sort of communication, but I really don't remember. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago. And it's like this, listen here. I don't think I had any connections with Obrenovic at one point. The connection was lost. I'm sure about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: The connection line was lost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you had connections, were there many exchanges between you and Mr. Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No. No. No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could be shown Exhibit 100 -- I believe 121. And while that's being done --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you were absent, somebody else for you would take over Lovac and communicate with whoever wanted to communicate with you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if page 7 of the English version could be put onto the ELMO, and -- in B/C/S. You'll be shown that page. Perhaps if you can see somewhere in the middle, Mr. Mihic, there is an entry in your B/C/S original and it says: "1825," "1825," and that's on the 14th July, "238 Lovac 1 - Lovac." Could you see that on your document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me read what it says. It says: "They were attacked there. They requested something to be sent. Is there anything," and then it says, "came interrupted (L1)." I take it that's Lovac 1. And then there is: "Igman informed Lovac what he (Vuk) came." Now, do you remember this conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's 14th July at 1825.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we see here Igman. Do you know who Igman was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't know. No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go down a few lines, about four lines, and it says, and I quote again: "On the frequency 293 at 2045 Igman 1 and Lovac 1 and Lovac - surround the forces with war materiel, reinforcement is coming from the Main Staff and now Mane's men are coming." Again it's Lovac involved, your call-sign. Do you remember - again, in the evening 14th July - do you remember this conversation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the conversation, but usually when I didn't pick up and when Lovac 1 talked to someone, as far as I remember he would usually use the Lovac codes -- call-sign without the number 1. So if Lovac and Lovac 1 have a conversation, then that's what they say. But if they talk to someone, they would just say Lovac because it was just the same unit. So the signalsman who was where I was, he would follow Lovac 1, and he would report with the call-sign Lovac. So I didn't have the need to involve myself. That's why you have Igman and Lovac. Why would Igman have talked to Lovac? And what am I? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these couple of conversations that we were discussing, you don't remember anything about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't remember any other conversation which would stick out in your mind on that day.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I do remember the conversation. I don't know what day it was exactly, but I do remember when the operations around Srebrenica started. The -- it was reported to the centre that there was a long column, and you couldn't see the end of the column. When the army platoon went for reconnaissance and reconnoitring, then that was the first information, when the scouts went out. So I received this information and conveyed it further on, of course. Who received it, I can't say; the signalsman down there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was an army platoon from the Zvornik Brigade who was down in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, no; not in Srebrenica. That was in the Zvornik portion, Lijesanj or somewhere around there, towards Glodina and Kamenica. That's where it was noticed. Now what the date was I don't know. You probably have the right information. You must have the date. But that was the first information I received, the first information that came in to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking back, that is the one conversation which would stick in your memory since today.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: I remember that well. It was the first one, and I know that exactly, for a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other conversation you recall now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With Your Honour's permission, just a few questions. Re-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mihic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one point during those days because of the intensity of the fighting that was going on you know that Obrenovic was in the field, on the spot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know whether Obrenovic during those days used a vehicle of some kind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He went with a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the make. It was a jeep of some kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he drive the jeep?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, no. He had a driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. He had a driver. Fine. Now, in the jeep was the signalsman there that was assigned to him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, from the crossroads leading to Snagovo, from Crni Vrh to the Zvornik Brigade, how far is that journey? How far is the route?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'd say about ten, 12, 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe it now gets out of the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. You began to ask some questions in some new areas. The re-examination should be within the scope of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. Just one more question, then, and I'll wind up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long does a vehicle take to get -- to pass that 10-12 route?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It takes 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point you said that from time to time you would have a bad connection, lose the connection with Obrenovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that show that he was moving around?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: It indicates that he was moving around, and maybe my battery was low. Maybe my battery was -- his battery was low and then he exchanged his battery somewhere in the battalion later on. So his battery was low, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also said at one point that you remember that on that day, the 14th or in the evening, that you lost all connection with Obrenovic. Is that right? Can you tell us or can you remember when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MIHIC
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
